extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, PTAB litigators, patent owners, petitioners, and IP counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance about how the PTAB categorizes its decisions under SOP 2 (routine, informative, representative, precedential), what those categories mean for bindingness and persuasion, and the process and considerations for designating precedential opinions. Useful for practitioners deciding which PTAB authorities to cite or follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB authority and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) is established under 35 U.S.C. § 6(a) and consists of administrative patent judges, a chief patent judge, and four ex officio members; the AIA authorizes the PTAB to conduct derivation proceedings (§135), IPRs and PGRs (chapters 31 and 32), and to hear appeals under § 134(a) and (b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes the PTAB's statutory competence to resolve certain disputes, and frames which proceedings and decisions fall within the PTAB's decision-making and designation regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: SOP 2: Four decision categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard Operating Procedure 2 (SOP 2) defines four categories of PTAB decisions: routine, informative, representative, and precedential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SOP 2 is the controlling administrative guidance for how the PTAB designates and treats its decisions; each category has different expectations for bindingness, persuasive value, and public prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine Decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly every PTAB decision and order have the default designation of routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine decisions become binding in that particular case until a subsequent PTAB decision, an expanded panel, or a reviewing court overturns it. They include procedural and substantive orders (interlocutory or final). Routine decisions are the 'daily work' outcomes and, while not generally precedential, can be cited and may gain persuasive force (e.g., frequently-cited routine opinions). Routine decisions can bind USPTO examiners for claims in the same family (e.g., canceled claims), and parties/boards must operate consistently with the decision in that case unless adjusted by a later PTAB panel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative Decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative opinions typically provide a representative sample of outcomes on a specific issue and are used to bring exemplary opinions to public attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative decisions are intended to highlight PTAB-preferred practices on new IPR/CBM issues and include categories such as representative trial hearing orders, institution decisions (e.g., denials applying §325(d)), scheduling orders, motions to amend guidance (including at least one grant), other orders (redundant grounds, pro hac vice, real-party-in-interest, §315(b) activity, joinder), notices (petition sufficiency/defects), settlement-related orders, and evidentiary/discovery orders. Representative opinions are not binding authority but serve as examples and guidance; practitioners unfamiliar with practice areas should consult them. (The article notes there were 46 decisions designated representative as of the cited date.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Informative Decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB designates certain decisions as informative and highlights them on its website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTAB may label a decision informative for any reason; common reasons include establishing suggested practices for frequently recurring issues, providing guidance on issues of first impression, or clarifying PTAB rules/practices. Informative opinions are not binding on the PTAB. They often address more substantive legal issues encountered less frequently than representative decisions. (The article notes 21 decisions designated informative as of the cited date.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedential Decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief judge may designate an opinion precedential after nomination and internal review; emphasis is placed on opinions resolving conflicts or addressing novel questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedential decisions are rare and are intended to resolve intra-PTAB conflicts or novel legal questions. As of the article's date only three AIA trial opinions had been designated precedential (SecureBuy v. CardinalCommerce; Westlake v. Credit Acceptance; LG Elecs. v. Mondis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process for designating precedential opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Any PTAB member may recommend an opinion for precedential status; any member of the public may request designation in writing within 60 days of issuance by forwarding reasons to the chief judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For opinions considered potentially precedential, the chief judge circulates the opinion to all PTAB members who have a limited period to vote and comment. If a majority of voting members agree, the chief judge notifies the Director; the Director must concur to finalize designation. No opinion can be made precedential without the Director's approval. The process is deliberate and can explain the scarcity of precedential designations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signatures and panel size do not alter designation status
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if more than three administrative patent judges sign an opinion (including dissents or expanded panels/rehearings), the opinion remains routine unless designated otherwise under SOP 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number of judges voting on or signing an opinion does not automatically elevate a decision's category; formal designation under SOP 2 is required to change its status to representative, informative, or precedential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasive weight vs. binding effect of categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative and informative decisions are not binding on the PTAB; routine decisions are binding in the particular case; precedential decisions are intended to bind and resolve conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should recognize the difference between binding effect and persuasive force. Frequently-cited routine decisions can carry persuasive weight across panels even without formal designation. Because the number of routine decisions is large, designation of more informative or representative opinions could improve predictability and save judicial resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical guidance for practitioners on using PTAB decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners should become familiar with the PTAB’s informative and precedential opinions and check for updates; use informative/precedential opinions as road maps and follow the 'great weight' of routine decisions for minor procedural matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly monitor PTAB-designated informative/representative/precedential opinions. Use representative/informative opinions to understand PTAB-preferred practices and to predict outcomes on particular facts. For minor procedural issues and situations unaddressed by higher authority, follow the body of routine decisions; citing frequently-applied routine opinions may be persuasive. Advocates may request precedential designation within 60 days to attempt formalization of guidance.
